To open it, you have to  discover concealed sliders and activate hidden mechanisms to unlock it. What makes it mine is creating a custom-designed puzzle system that will use intricate mechanisms that I will design in CAD and bring to life through 3D printing.

### 2026-10-15 – # Oct 14th, Starting LOCKBOX

**3h**

# Oct 14th, Starting LOCKBOX

Today, I started working on my CAD project, Lockbox, a minimalist, 3D-printed puzzle vault behind a series of mechanical locks. My goal is to create something that looks like a simple cube from the outside but contains a complex locking system on the inside. Instead of using a conventional key lock, the vault will require users to push and pull certain joints in the correct sequence to open it.

Before starting the actual model, I wanted to research mechanical locks and puzzle boxes to understand how their components work together. I wanted to make sure the mechanisms were realistic enough to manufacture with a 3D printer rather than simply designing something that looks interesting

## Tutorials and Research
After a bit of research into what CAD software I would use, I decided on Fusion 360 for it's assembly functions. I then started by exploring Fusion 360 tutorials focused on mechanical design and assemblies. I watched the full 1 hour 30 minuteLEARN FUSION 360 FAST! A Beginner Tutorial – Complete Lecture video by Benjamin Leitgib. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mK60ROb2RKI
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/4843e5de62359bdea1585038458f8d290e97c734554f2c000610199a82a099e7.png)

After watching the video, I recreated the project myself in fusion360 to understand the different features for the software. The video covered creating separate components, applying joints, and testing movement within an assembly. Which is important for Lockbox because the rotating dials, sliding panels, and internal bolts need to move independently while remaining properly aligned with the rest of the design.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/74fd4308b829636c8172cdeefb10f838ab02d134458bad318fec2032aceda883.png)

I also studied the  How to Design a 3D Printed Twist Lock Lid in Fusion 360 by Send to Print. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C6kF1huqRMU
This tutorial shows how to design a twist-lock mechanism, adjust clearances between parts, and test whether the printed components fit correctly. I learned that even simple locking mechanism  need careful attention to dimensions, especially tolerances. Parts that fit perfectly in a digital model may not necessarily move smoothly when 3D printed.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/bb12db6770b7f71b6fb747c7d27e47119b5cf59004fc65405cfd3c105cd9ece6.png)

# Initial Design Planning
 After researching the mechanisms, I started outlining how the vault would work. My current concept is a cube , with a hollow interior large enough to store small objects. I want the exterior to remain minimalist, using flat surfaces, subtle chamfers, and concealed seams so that the opening mechanism isn't obvious.

I also began planning a possible unlocking sequence involving several connected puzzles:
1. A Hidden slider: A concealed panel reveals the first control.
2. A Rotating symbol dial: Aligning specific symbols releases another mechanism.
3. The Final locking bolt: Completing the previous steps allows the lid to open.

These are preliminary ideas and I still need to determine how each component will connect as well as how one puzzle will enable the next.

# Next Steps
My next goal is to begin modeling the outer shell in Fusion 360 and establish the dimensions of the interior. After that, I plan to design and test one locking mechanism separately before integrating it into the complete vault. I will also need to account for 3D-printing tolerances and the possibility of a mechanism becoming jammed.

Today was mainly about researching the engineering behind the project and turning a general concept into a workable plan. I now understand how to use the app and have a better understanding of the mechanical principles I need to develop to bring Lockbox to life.

### 2026-10-18 – # Oct 17th, The beginning of the build for LOCKBOX

**4h**

# Oct 17th, The beginning of the build for LOCKBOX

Today, I continued working on my CAD project, Lockbox, by focusing on building the mechanical systems that would make the vault work. My main goal was to start understanding the actual components I would need to create this system now that I understand how to use fusion 360. Since I wanted the outside of the Lockbox to look simple and minimalistic, the hard part would be from fitting all the internal mechanisms.

I decided the most effective thing to do was to practice building each individual mechanism before putting them all in the box. This would help me identify the design problems early and make it easier to modify individual components without having to rebuild the entire assembly.

## Researching building Mechanical Locking Systems

I began by researching different types of lock mechanisms and focused on three main designs: sliding bolts, twist locks, and rotating combination dials. Each mechanism offers a different way to prevent the vault from opening and understanding them helped me determine which would be most suitable for my project.

A sliding bolt works by moving a rigid component into or out of a locking positions and when engaged the bold prevents a panel from moving. This design is pretty simple and can be made easily as a 3d model making it a good first candidate for my prototype

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/a0018d4b98644a14a27f35f35ca229fe5b9aa6bbd4159598d8b66ddf684c6e22.png)

I also looked at twist-lock mechanisms. These could be useful for a hidden dial on the Lockbox. Their main challenge is making sure the parts rotate smoothly when locked.

Finally, I considered rotating combination dials. These could make the vault more interactive by making the user align symbols before the vault is opened. I like this idea because it introduces an actual puzzle-solving element.

After comparing these options, I decided that a sliding bolt would be an easy starting point because it's simpler to prototype than a complete combination lock.

## Planning the Dimensions

Then, I start planning the vault's overall dimensions with approximately 3mm thick walls. I considered how much interior space would be available for storage and how the lid would connect to the main body. I also need to leave enough room for the locking mechanisms without interfering with the outside.

I want to keep the outside minimal with concealed seems and no obvious signs of how the vault opens.

## Planning the Dimensions

Then, I started planning the vault's overall dimensions with approximately 3mm thick walls. I considered how much interior space would be available for storage and how the lid would connect to the main body. I also need to leave enough room for the locking mechanisms without interfering with the outside.

I want to keep the outside minimal with concealed seems and no obvious signs of how the vault opens.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/9c02408f351053707cefbc076b05b251c3514480131255bb588b8a28d0b53796.png)

## Modelling mechanisms in Fusion 360
I started exploring how to model moving mechanical components in Fusion 360. My initial focus was a sliding bolt and its guide channel. The bolt needs to move smoothly while remaining properly aligned.

I also learned why designing components separately is important. When I tried building my bolt mechanism to fit inside the dimensions of the cube, it just wouldn't fit. Eventually I gave up and moved into into another file but keeping the bolt and housing individually made it easier to adjust the dimensions later while still testing their movements so eventually I could just scale it down and made it fit properly.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/ca16d61198bfc7e2cbaaa54454aaadce27072d6602d7afe5c6ccce7ab27c6dc1.png)

## Developing the outer shell

I also planned how to model the outer shell. I built a hollow interior that needed to remain strong enough to  remain rigid enough to support the locking system. I considered using Fusion 360's Shell tool or an extruded cut to create the cavity.

Another consideration is tolerances for 3d printing so I need to test different clearances and adjust the design accordingly. Below is a screenshot of the cube after I finished modeling it.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/0770cb9c92b0143f40f01de4543f8ba04c6fd11ed78b9e8fbb899a86de46f522.png)

## Summary
I researched the internal mechanisms, sketched out the design measurements for Lockbox,  practiced building a slide and bolt lock in fusion 360 and built the casing for Lockbox.

## Next Steps
My next goal is to develop the outer shell and refine the sliding bolt into a working prototype. Aftertesting the basic mechanism, I plan on exploring more complicated features and hopefully avoid problems when actually completing Lockbox.

### 2026-10-18 – # Oct 18th - Day 3 Developing the mechanisms

**3h**

# Oct 18th - Day 3 Developing the mechanisms

Today, I focused on refining the dimensions of my lockbox and developing two important parts of the design: a sliding dovetail lid and an internal combination lock. Since my goal is to create a functional vault that I can 3d print, I needed to consider how the individual parts would fit together without getting stuck.

# Redesigning the dimensions

I decided to change the dimensions of the lockbox and shrink to 150 x 150 x 150mm. I was worried about clearance issues since the box would have a lot of moving components. Making it smaller would make it more manageable to print but I also needed to make sure there would be enough space on the inside for the locking mechanism. I considered how the wall thickness, lid and internal components would affect the available space. Since 3d-printed parts aren't always accurate, I needed to account for small gaps between components.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/84dbebb84cf5168d5ffd67392276fdad63488ddd03e0e32d604c3e530dd4b24a.png)

# Designing a sliding dovetail lid

The first mechanism I tried building today was a sliding dovetail lid which unlike a regular lid uses interlocking edges to slide of off a specific path. I wanted to use this mechanism because it seems like a more interesting way to open the box. The lid and main body would need matching profiles to move smoothly and I also considered how the sliding distance would affect the design.

When modelling this in fusion 360, I had to remind myself to think about clearance. If the edges are too tight, friction would keep the lid stuck but if they were too loose the lid would just slide out. I had to account for these tolerances where preparing the design.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/4339eddc354b546057e962ebb828b8517fa9383e68c26cdad6a6314f28da1d32.png)

#  Developing an Internal Combination Lock

The second mechanism I worked on was an internal combination lock. My goal is to make the box require more than simply sliding the lid open. Instead the user should have to discover and enter the correct combination before the lock opens.

The basic concept uses rotating parts that align to open a locking bar but block the bar when the combination is wrong.  Designing this mechanism meant careful consideration for how the pieces would rotate. I also needed to make sure the lock can fit inside my lockbox and that it would actually work without jamming

I still need to refine the exact combination mechanism and test it's movement but for now I've built a semi function out of scale design that reliably works.
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/a75a75faf7e657631f61705841cd6fe9aacc33a241770dd871919714e179bf4c.png)

## Summary

I redid my dimensions for the lockbox for a more accurate, safer version that has better clearances as well as model two important mechanisms for the box itself: a dovetail lid and combination lock.

## Next steps

My next goal is to add all my separate mechanisms into the exterior casing to create the Lockbox. the combination lock controls the locking bar to control the lid which opens the box.

Once I connect these components I need to check that these is enough room inside the 150mm cube for this all to fit. I also plan on testing the moving parts to adjust clearances but overall it's time to wrap up this project and put it all together.

### 2026-10-18 – # Lockbox Oct 18 - Starting from scratch

**6h**

# Lockbox Oct 18 - Starting from scratch

Today, my goal was to take the three separate files I had for Lockbox and put them into my outer casing, but I quickly ran into trouble. My components wouldn't fit together and after much back and forth I had no other option but to give up with little time. Thus I had to quickly decide a way to design LOCKBOX before the week was over. Ultimately, I decided to look online for ideas when I found my solution: Building the LOCKBOX using only sliding mechanisms and so I began a quick last minute grind for the entire day to finish my project.

## Main body and base

I started by designing the main body of the puzzle box but since I ran into scaling issues before, I decided the best thing to do was make a design based on my gut, before adapting the other parts to fit it, and then from there deciding the scale during printing. I approached the new design as a collection of different panels instead of trying to create the entire box as one object.

In Fusion 360, I started working with sketches, using ideas that I saw on google, to decide the shapes of the panels before extruding them. Keeping the panels separate made it easier to examine how they would connect during assembly. The main body needed to provide enough internal space to store objects while also supporting the other components. So I had to consider the thickness of the walls and made this part as the reference for the rest of the design because the other panels needed to align with it.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/ec90a2cce0592a5710d8ffa629eaf9e100886ae731c1282790296fb9a0b31c1b.png)

For the main body, I kept and simple and planned on adding external side walls as well as inner side walls, as well as a lid, so I really only kept 2 sides and the bottom. I wanted to add screw head type locks like I had seen online, so I added indents for those on the inside of the base and wanted to add screw head extrusions on the side walls.

## Side Panels

The side panels form the walls of the box but instead of modeling every wall as part of one solid body, I designed the panels as separate pieces. This made the model easier to organize.

For the Side panels, I made them symmetrical and gave them an upside down L shape. The only difference was that they would have an overhang. I created the L shape in a sketch before extruding it. Then I sketched 3 screw heads before extruding them and building the caps after that. From there I wanted to mirror the side that I just made to get both sides, which gave me the two halves I needed.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/61674b2c385dd070c33c243d80b5c41dda9b8953e040dcfd0b476253180e78b6.png)

## Inner Side Panels

For the inner side panels, I wanted to make something more complex so my puzzle box would be an actual puzzle but at the same time I learned from my mistake of overshoot so I decided to go simple. I sketched an E shape before adding a top rail and a thinner bottom rail that would just needs to be slided to move. This way it's a simple mechanism but harder for people to solve without actually knowing the puzzle. From there just like before I went really simple and mirrored the panels to give me my two sides.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/3ac30099e7b291d246c8bd453db227d0429a0b5671e985be7636e024b90da656.png)

## Outer casing and lid.

Now that I had most of my puzzle setup, I needed to give it that minimalist look that made it hard to tell that it was a puzzle but also to hide the inside slides, so the people solving it couldn't actually just see what they needed to do. For this I just made an outside case that was big enough to fit the side panels and the main body. I used what I learned about dovetail joints from before and decided to make the lid with a dovetail joint. The lid itself was also really simple essentially just being a rectangle top with a trapezoid connector for the outer casing to give it a smooth look that nobody could tell.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/99b76fdf494f7cd21516394d27514c3021b6fae4c07e58599e98a0cbeb5acd39.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/65807804ae74fdb08b7590a1a5a135bf8cf434419331ffc8ce21ff390cc22048.png)

## The Bar
The final last project was something I called the bar, it was just a simple rectangle that I sketched in a square bracket shape [, before extruding it and putting a notch in the middle that would connect to the inner main body. To separate the components and make things better, I incorporated one notch into outer body and another into the bar so that you have to add both before fitting the inner case in, or when solving the case, the bar would have to be removed to take out the outer body to remove the side panels to finally get to the inside.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/698e6e3ea840c74cccc54330f2406d64fbdb5cdfd325cec423a890635ca8f8ec.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/1f39f39fba965b3424cde9185e5d9cf3e9127bbe3ac6ea9d62f1d60ae6e76d92.png)

## Finished

And so with the idea of creating simple sliding pieces that fit together, I just built piece after piece before deciding how to make them fit together, while trying to keep things simpler so I wouldn't run into the same issue as before, where my separate components were too rigid and unable to mesh together. this time I had gone the opposite, separate components that i build for and decide how to fit them together as I work my way through. It took a chunk out of my morning and some late night grinding but I finally got it done. With this my LOCKBOX is done, and finally I can print something to stop my little brother from stealing my stuff.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/b3b76438229ca1f644d914a81152d7d6a6f659cadf676a83e9b1dcbaaf9ff5bc.png)

# Summary

LOCKBOX was a CAD and 3D-printing project where I designed a minimalist puzzle box to store personal belongings while hiding its locking mechanism. My original design included more complex mechanisms like a combination dial, but I ran into assembly issues when trying to combine my separate STL files in Fusion 360. With my deadline approaching, I decided to start from scratch and redesign the box using simpler sliding mechanisms.

I built the new design piece by piece, including the main body, symmetrical side panels, inner sliding panels, outer casing, lid, and locking bar. Using sketches, extrusions, mirroring, and dovetail joints in Fusion 360, I created separate components designed to fit together. By focusing on simplicity, I managed to finish the design before the week was over while keeping the minimalist appearance and hidden locking mechanism I originally wanted.

# What I Learned

Throughout this project, I learned the importance of accurate measurements, scaling, and planning how components will fit together before designing complex mechanisms. My original mistake was focusing too much on individual parts without considering how they would interact. I also gained experience using Fusion 360 tools, including building bodies, components and assemblies, while learning to consider the clearances and tolerances required for 3D printing.

Most importantly, I learned to adapt when things do not go according to plan. Rather than wasting more time trying to fix an overly complicated design, I researched alternatives on google and simplified the project to meet my deadline. This taught me how to find practical solutions and learn from my mistakes to build something that could actually work.
